why_angle: The cited pages compare 3–5 kW inverters by watts and price only. None of them says that the Solis S6 5 kW hybrid accepts only a 120–500 V high-voltage battery, so it cannot use the common 48 V (51.2 V) rack packs. None says that the $2,998 Sol-Ark 5K split-phase is off-grid only in California and Hawaii. So none shows which inverter and battery together actually fit under $3,000. This page sorts every candidate by the battery it runs on and prices the full inverter-plus-battery system.

page.desc: Solar hybrid inverters under $3,000 compared by the battery they run on: a 6.5 kW 120/240 V 48 V unit plus 10.24 kWh of batteries costs $2,988, and the Solis S6 needs a 120–500 V pack.
page.answer: Short answer. The best solar hybrid inverter under $3,000 is the Sun Gold Power SPH6548P. It delivers 6,500 W at 120/240 V from a 48 V battery and costs $1,035, so two 48 V 5.12 kWh batteries still fit the budget ($2,988 total). The 5000W Solis S6 hybrid needs a 120–500 V battery instead.

page.after:
What the differences mean

  • Inverter plus battery under $3,000: the SPH6548P and two 51.2 V 100 Ah server-rack packs cost $1,035 + $1,953 = $2,988. That buys 6.5 kW of 120/240 V output and 2 × 5.12 kWh = 10.24 kWh of storage.
  • Budget left for a battery: $3,000 − $1,035 = $1,965 (SPH6548P), $3,000 − $1,229 = $1,771 (Solis), $3,000 − $1,499.99 = $1,500.01 (EG4 6000XP), $3,000 − $2,998 = $2 (Sol-Ark 5K split phase).
  • Cost per rated watt: SPH6548P $1,035 ÷ 6,500 W = $0.16/W; Solis $1,229 ÷ 5,000 W = $0.25/W; EG4 $1,499.99 ÷ 6,000 W = $0.25/W; Rich Solar NOVA MAX 3K $799.99 ÷ 3,000 W = $0.27/W; Sol-Ark 5K split $2,998 ÷ 5,000 W = $0.60/W.
  • Larger option if you only need the inverter: Sun Gold Power's 10KW 48V split-phase unit costs $1,422, or $1,422 ÷ 10,000 W = $0.14/W. Adding the same two batteries brings the total to $1,422 + $1,953 = $3,375, which is over the $3,000 cap.

Battery voltage decides what you can pair

A hybrid inverter's battery port accepts one voltage family. The figure that sets your total cost is that range, not the inverter price. There are three families on this list:

  • 48 V (51.2 V LiFePO4): SPH6548P, EG4 6000XP and both Sol-Ark 5K versions. These units take common server-rack packs. Sun Gold Power lists its SG48100P (51.2 V, 100 Ah, UL 1973 / UL 9540A) as compatible with SunGoldPower, Deye, Growatt, Victron and other inverters over CAN/RS485. The two-pack costs $1,953 at the maker {buy:sungoldpower-sg48100p-2-pack}.
  • High voltage (120–500 V): Solis S6-EH1P5K-H-US. A 48 V pack runs at 51.2 V nominal, which is 51.2 ÷ 120 = 43% of the Solis minimum, so it will not work at all. Solis's US support site also says that its high-voltage hybrids do not support open-loop batteries and that an unverified battery can void the inverter warranty. You need a closed-loop HV stack from Solis's matching list. In return, the Solis is the only inverter here that lists UL 1741 SB and California Rule 21 for grid export, and it makes native 120/240 V backup power.
  • 24 V: Rich Solar NOVA MAX 3K. It suits RV and cabin banks, gives 120 V from one unit, and needs paralleled units for split phase.

There are two Sol-Ark 5K listings at the same store. The $2,998 split-phase unit is, in RENVU's words, 'not CEC listed (CA) nor HECO compliant (HI). Offgrid only in these markets.' The $1,486 single-phase 5K is 'Perfect for 120V only setups', so it won't run a 240 V well pump or dryer. The SPH6548P's UL 1741 listing is worded for off-grid systems. If your utility must approve grid export, the Solis is the one on this list that lists Rule 21 and IEEE 1547.

Not recommended

SMA Sunny Boy 5.0 (SB5.0-1SP-US-41). It is a grid-tie string inverter with no battery input, and Solar-Electric.com marks it 'discontinued' and 'at End of life'. It cannot store solar for night use or run a battery-backed system. If you want backup, pick one of the hybrids above.
